questions.q: Information is
o: data that has been processed and given meaning
questions.why: Data + context = information.

questions.q: Batch processing suits
questions.why: Real-time processing suits bookings and control.

questions.q: Which is an example of information rather than data?
o: The average temperature this week was 31 °C
A list of numbers with no labels
questions.why: Information is data given context and meaning.

questions.q: What is the defining distinction between data and information?
o: Data is always numerical while information is alphabetical
Information is data that has been processed and given context and meaning
Data is only stored in RAM while information is on disk
questions.why: Data consists of raw symbols or figures with no inherent meaning; once structured in context, it becomes actionable information.

questions.q: A sales report is produced using customer figures collected three years ago. Which factor affecting the quality of information is the main problem?
questions.why: Old data may no longer reflect the current situation, so the information's age lowers its quality even if the figures were accurate when collected.

long.q: Compare batch processing and real-time processing, giving a suitable use for each.
scheme: B1: batch: data collected and processed together later, without user interaction
B1: use: payroll / utility bills
B1: real-time: data processed immediately as it arrives
B1: use: booking systems / control systems

long.q: Distinguish between static data and dynamic data, giving one practical business example of each.
scheme: B1: static data does not change once created / rarely updated (e.g. title, date of birth, fixed product ID)
B1: dynamic data changes frequently / updated continuously in response to events
B1: practical example of dynamic data (e.g. current stock levels, bank account balance, flight seat availability)

long.q: Compare symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
scheme: B1: symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and to decrypt
B1: the key must be shared safely between sender and receiver, which is a risk if it is intercepted
B1: asymmetric encryption uses a pair of keys: a public key to encrypt and a matching private key to decrypt
B1: the private key is never shared, so it is more secure for key exchange, but it is slower; symmetric is faster for large amounts of data

long.q: A council wants to find out how many vehicles use a road each day. Describe one direct and one indirect source of this data, and give an advantage of each.
scheme: B1: direct source: data collected first-hand for this purpose, e.g. a traffic counter or sensor on the road, or a person counting vehicles
B1: advantage: the council knows exactly how it was collected; it is up to date and only relevant data is collected
B1: indirect source: data originally collected for another purpose, e.g. traffic-camera records, satellite-navigation company data, a previous survey
B1: advantage: it is already available, so it is quicker and cheaper to obtain; may cover a longer period

long.q: Describe four factors that affect the quality of information.
scheme: B1: accuracy: errors in the data lead to wrong information
B1: relevance: the information must meet the user's needs; irrelevant detail wastes time
B1: age (timeliness): out-of-date information may no longer be true
B1: e.g. level of detail: too much or too little detail; completeness: missing parts make it less useful

questions.q: A compiler
o: translates the whole program before it runs
translates line by line as it runs
questions.why: An interpreter works line by line.

questions.q: A device driver is:
o: Software that lets the operating system communicate with a hardware device
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the most common mistake was to consider a device driver to be hardware.

questions.q: Which software controls the hardware and provides a user interface?
questions.why: Device drivers let the operating system talk to particular hardware.

questions.q: Which software is classified as utility system software rather than application software?
questions.why: Utility software maintains, analyses, and optimises computer performance and disk storage, rather than carrying out user-directed tasks.

questions.q: Why might a small business choose off-the-shelf software rather than custom-written software?
o: It will meet every one of the business's exact requirements
It is cheaper and available to use straight away
The business will own the source code
It is written specially for the business by its own programmers
questions.why: Off-the-shelf software's development cost is shared by many buyers and it is ready immediately; custom-written software fits exact needs but is expensive and slow to produce.

long.q: Compare a compiler and an interpreter.
scheme: B1: a compiler translates the whole source code into machine code before it runs
B1: it produces an executable that runs without the translator, and runs faster
B1: an interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time
B1: it stops at the first error, which helps debugging, but the program runs more slowly and needs the interpreter every time

long.q: Explain what a device driver is and why an operating system needs one for each printer model.
scheme: B1: a device driver is system software that lets the operating system communicate with a hardware device
B1: it translates the operating system's general commands into the specific instructions the device understands
B1: each printer model works differently, so the operating system needs the correct driver for that model to control it

long.q: A business needs software to manage its orders. Compare buying off-the-shelf software with having custom-written software developed.
scheme: B1: off-the-shelf software is cheaper, as the development cost is shared among many buyers
B1: it is available at once and well tested, with plenty of support, training and user forums
B1: custom-written software is designed exactly for the business's needs, with no unnecessary features
B1: but it is expensive and takes a long time to develop, and may contain bugs at first

long.q: Compare a mainframe computer with a supercomputer, giving a typical use of each.
scheme: B1: a mainframe handles very large numbers of users and transactions at the same time, with high reliability
B1: use of a mainframe, e.g. processing bank transactions, census data, airline bookings
B1: a supercomputer has thousands of processors working in parallel to carry out complex calculations as fast as possible (measured in FLOPS)
B1: use of a supercomputer, e.g. weather forecasting, climate modelling, scientific research, simulations

long.q: Describe what disk defragmentation software does and explain why it is not used on a solid-state drive (SSD).
scheme: B1: over time, files are stored in fragments scattered over different parts of a hard disk
B1: defragmentation moves the fragments so each file is stored in adjacent blocks and free space is grouped together
B1: the read/write head moves less, so files are read faster from a hard disk
B1: an SSD has no moving parts, so access time doesn't depend on where data is stored, and the extra writes would shorten its life

questions.q: In a control system, an actuator
o: carries out a physical action, e.g. opens a window
questions.why: Sensors measure; actuators act.

questions.q: In a computer-controlled greenhouse, what does the microprocessor do with a sensor reading?
o: Compares it with a preset value and switches an actuator if needed
questions.why: Monitoring only records; control acts on the readings in a feedback loop.

questions.q: Why is an ADC needed in many monitoring systems?
o: Sensors give analogue signals that the computer must receive in digital form
questions.why: A DAC is used when the computer drives an analogue device.

questions.q: What component is required to convert continuous physical sensor signals into digital data for a microprocessor?
questions.why: Real-world variables like temperature or pressure vary continuously; an ADC samples these into discrete binary values for computer processing.

questions.q: Which of these is a monitoring system rather than a control system?
o: A heating system that switches a boiler on when a room is cold
Automatic traffic lights that change when cars are detected
A greenhouse that opens its windows when it is too warm
A hospital system that records a patient's pulse and sounds an alarm if it goes too high
questions.why: A monitoring system only records and reports readings, warning a person when needed; a control system uses the readings to change the process through actuators.

long.q: A greenhouse uses a computer to control temperature. Describe how the system works.
scheme: B1: a temperature sensor measures temperature continuously
B1: an ADC converts the analogue reading to digital
B1: the microprocessor compares the reading with a preset value
B1: if too high, it sends a signal to an actuator to open a window / start a fan
B1: the process repeats continuously (feedback)

long.q: Explain why sensors in a monitoring system need calibrating, and describe how a temperature sensor could be calibrated.
scheme: B1: sensor readings can drift or be inaccurate, so the measurements recorded would be wrong
B1: the sensor is placed in conditions of known temperature, e.g. melting ice at 0 °C, or alongside an accurate reference thermometer
B1: its readings are compared with the known values
B1: the system is adjusted (an offset or scale set) so the readings match; using two known points corrects both offset and scale

long.q: Explain the difference between a computer monitoring system and a computer control system, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: a monitoring system takes readings from sensors and records or displays them, possibly with warnings, but does not change the conditions
B1: an example, e.g. monitoring a patient's heart rate; a weather station; pollution monitoring
B1: a control system uses the sensor readings to make decisions and sends signals to actuators to change conditions (feedback)
B1: an example, e.g. a central-heating system; traffic lights; an automatic greenhouse

long.q: A house has a computer-controlled burglar alarm with infrared and pressure sensors. Describe how the system detects an intruder and responds.
scheme: B1: the system is set (armed) by entering a code, and the sensors send data continuously to the microprocessor
B1: an infrared sensor detects body heat/movement in a room; a pressure sensor detects someone standing on a mat or floor
B1: the analogue readings are converted to digital by an ADC
B1: the microprocessor compares the readings with preset values
B1: if a reading is outside the preset value, it sends signals to sound a siren and flash lights, and may call the owner or police

long.q: Patients in an intensive care unit are monitored by computer. Name two sensors that would be used and give two advantages of computer monitoring over nurses taking readings.
scheme: B1: a sensor, e.g. pulse/heart-rate sensor
B1: a second sensor, e.g. blood-pressure, temperature or blood-oxygen sensor
B1: an advantage, e.g. readings are taken continuously, 24 hours a day, without nurses getting tired
B1: a second advantage, e.g. an alarm sounds at once if a reading goes outside safe limits; readings are more accurate and are stored and graphed automatically; nurses are free for other tasks

questions.q: In a flowchart, a decision is shown by
questions.why: Rectangles are processes; parallelograms are input/output.

questions.q: In a flowchart, a decision box must have:
o: A Yes and a No output
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates are reminded every decision box needs Yes and No outputs, using mathematical expressions rather than text.

questions.q: Which flowchart symbol shows a decision?
o: A diamond with Yes and No exits
questions.why: Examiners (2023): every decision box needs a Yes and a No output.

questions.q: What is the primary role of a dry run using a trace table in algorithm development?
o: To manually track variable values step by step and identify logic errors
To convert source code into machine code
To test the clock speed of the processor
questions.why: A trace table allows a programmer to test an algorithm by hand with test data to verify logic before coding.

questions.q: What is output? X ← 3 ; Y ← 0 ; WHILE X < 20 DO Y ← Y + 1 ; X ← X * 2 ENDWHILE ; OUTPUT Y
questions.why: X goes from 3 to 6, 12 and then 24, adding 1 to Y each time; 24 < 20 is false, so the loop stops with Y = 3.

long.q: Draw a flowchart that inputs the marks of 20 students one at a time and, for each, outputs 'Pass' if the mark is 50 or more, otherwise 'Fail'.
scheme: B1: start and stop terminators
B1: a counter set to 0 and incremented each time
B1: input of the mark in a parallelogram
B1: decision Mark >= 50 with Yes/No branches to the correct outputs
B1: a loop back until 20 marks have been processed

long.q: An algorithm in pseudocode is: Total ← 0, Count ← 0, INPUT Num; WHILE Num <> -1: Total ← Total + Num, Count ← Count + 1, INPUT Num; ENDWHILE; OUTPUT Total / Count. The inputs are 4, 7, 10, -1. State the final values of Total and Count, the value output, and the purpose of the value -1.
scheme: B1: Total = 21
B1: Count = 3
B1: output 7 (21 ÷ 3), the average of the numbers entered
B1: -1 is a rogue (sentinel) value that ends the loop and is not included in the total

long.q: State what each of these flowchart symbols represents: (a) a rounded rectangle (terminator); (b) a parallelogram; (c) a rectangle; (d) a diamond.
scheme: B1: (a) start or stop of the algorithm
B1: (b) input or output
B1: (c) a process, e.g. a calculation or assignment
B1: (d) a decision, with two exits such as Yes/No

long.q: Write an algorithm in pseudocode that inputs 10 numbers and outputs the largest.
scheme: B1: the first number is input and stored as Largest (or Largest set to a very small value)
B1: a loop that runs the correct number of times, e.g. FOR Count ← 2 TO 10
B1: inputs a number inside the loop
B1: IF Num > Largest THEN Largest ← Num
B1: OUTPUT Largest after the loop ends

long.q: Explain the difference between a WHILE…ENDWHILE loop and a REPEAT…UNTIL loop.
scheme: B1: a WHILE loop tests its condition at the start, before the loop body
B1: so its body may not run at all if the condition is false at the start
B1: a REPEAT…UNTIL loop tests its condition at the end, so the body always runs at least once
B1: WHILE continues while the condition is true; REPEAT continues until the condition becomes true

questions.q: Which is a safety risk rather than a health risk?
questions.why: Safety risks cause accidents.

questions.q: Which is a way to reduce the risk of repetitive strain injury?
o: Use a wrist rest and take regular breaks
questions.why: Health risks need health measures, not security measures.

questions.q: What is phishing?
o: Hacking a Wi-Fi password by guessing
Fake messages that try to trick people into giving personal details
questions.why: Check the sender and never follow links asking for passwords.

questions.q: Which ergonomic measure helps prevent Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) for keyboard workers?
o: Using wrist rests and maintaining wrists straight with forearms parallel to desk
questions.why: RSI in wrists and fingers is mitigated by ergonomic wrist supports, correct elbow height, and regular short breaks.

questions.q: Before entering card details on a shopping website, which check best shows that the connection is encrypted?
o: The address begins with https and the browser shows a padlock
The website has lots of product photos
questions.why: https and the padlock show that TLS is encrypting data between the browser and the server; the other features say nothing about security.

long.q: Explain the difference between a health risk and a safety risk when using IT, giving one example of each and a precaution for each.
scheme: B1: a health risk harms the body over time, e.g. RSI or eye strain
B1: a precaution, e.g. regular breaks; ergonomic keyboard; anti-glare screen
B1: a safety risk can cause injury at once, e.g. electrocution, fire from overloaded sockets, tripping over cables
B1: a precaution, e.g. cable ducts; not overloading sockets; a CO₂ extinguisher nearby

long.q: Describe the difference between a virus, a worm and a Trojan horse.
scheme: B1: a virus is malicious code attached to a program or file that replicates when the infected file is run, often damaging data
B1: a worm is a standalone program that replicates and spreads across a network by itself, using up bandwidth and resources
B1: a Trojan horse pretends to be useful software but carries hidden malware, e.g. opening a backdoor; it does not replicate itself

long.q: Describe four precautions a teenager should take to stay safe when using social networking sites.
scheme: B1: set the profile to private so only approved friends can see posts
B1: do not give out personal details such as home address, school, phone number or live location
B1: only accept friend requests from people known in real life, and never meet an online contact alone
B1: e.g. think before posting photos, as they are permanent; report and block bullying or inappropriate contact; use a strong password

long.q: Explain what is meant by sensitive personal data, give two examples, and explain why it needs extra protection.
scheme: B1: personal data that could cause serious harm or discrimination if it were disclosed
B1: an example, e.g. ethnic or racial origin, religion
B1: a second example, e.g. health or medical records, political views, sexual orientation, criminal record, biometric data
B1: if leaked it could lead to discrimination, blackmail, embarrassment or identity theft

long.q: Explain how a keylogger can be used to steal a user's online banking details, and describe two ways of protecting against it.
scheme: B1: a keylogger is spyware that secretly records every key pressed
B1: the record is sent to the criminal, who finds the user's login name and password
B1: protection, e.g. up-to-date anti-spyware/anti-malware that detects and removes it
B1: a second protection, e.g. the bank asks for selected characters by drop-down menus or an on-screen keyboard; two-factor authentication

questions.q: The digital divide is
o: the gap between those with and without access to technology
questions.why: Caused by income, location, age, education.

questions.q: What is the digital divide?
o: The split between hardware and software
The gap between people who have access to IT and the internet and those who don't
questions.why: Causes include income, location, age and education.

questions.q: Which would most help to reduce the digital divide in a rural area?
o: Providing affordable broadband and community IT access
questions.why: Access and skills both matter.

questions.q: Which factor is a primary cause of the digital divide between rural and urban populations?
o: Urban citizens having higher CPU clock speeds
Rural residents refusing to use electronic currency
Unequal access to high-speed broadband telecommunications infrastructure
questions.why: Rural and remote areas often lack physical optical fibre infrastructure and 5G cellular coverage due to commercial unviability.

questions.q: Which is a likely consequence of the digital divide for people without internet access?
o: They may miss online job adverts, services and cheaper online prices
They always pay the same prices as everyone else
They gain easier access to online government services
questions.why: As more jobs, services and discounts move online, people who cannot get online are left at a disadvantage, which widens the gap.

long.q: Explain two causes of the digital divide within a country, and one way a government could reduce it.
scheme: B1: a cause, e.g. income: poorer households can't afford devices or broadband
B1: a second cause, e.g. location: rural areas lack broadband infrastructure; age or education: lack of digital skills
B1: a measure, e.g. funding rural broadband; subsidised devices; free digital-skills courses
B1: explained: how it gives the excluded group access or skills

long.q: Describe four effects the digital divide can have on people without access to the internet.
scheme: B1: fewer job opportunities, as jobs are often advertised and applied for online
B1: educational disadvantage, as homework, research and online courses need internet access
B1: paying more, as online prices and discounts are missed
B1: e.g. harder to use government and banking services that have moved online; social isolation from friends and family

long.q: Explain how mobile technology could help to reduce the digital divide between developed and developing countries.
scheme: B1: mobile networks are cheaper and quicker to build than cable or fibre broadband, especially in rural areas
B1: smartphones are cheaper than computers, so more people can afford to go online
B1: example: mobile banking lets people without a bank branch nearby send and receive money
B1: example: people can get education, health or weather/market information on their phones

long.q: Discuss the digital divide between older and younger people in a country.
scheme: B1: many older people did not grow up with computers and lack the skills or confidence to use them
B1: some fear online fraud or see no benefit, so they do not use online services
B1: this can leave them isolated and unable to use services that are now mainly online
B1: e.g. it can be reduced by free training at libraries or by family; however many older people are now online, so the gap is narrowing

long.q: A government plans to give a free laptop to every student from a low-income family. Evaluate whether this will close the digital divide for these students.
scheme: B1: students can do homework, research and online learning at home, removing an educational disadvantage
B1: they gain digital skills that will help them get jobs later
B1: but a laptop is of little use without affordable broadband or a mobile data connection at home
B1: students and parents may need training and technical support, and laptops need repair and replacing
B1: a reasoned conclusion, e.g. it reduces but does not close the divide unless connectivity and skills are also funded

questions.q: What does a VPN do?
o: creates an encrypted connection over a public network
questions.why: Virtual private network.

questions.q: What does a router do?
o: Connects devices in a LAN by broadcasting to all
Forwards data packets between different networks using IP addresses
questions.why: Examiners (2023): there was confusion between switches, routers and hubs.

questions.q: What does a switch do in a LAN?
o: Sends data only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses
Connects the LAN to the internet
questions.why: A hub sends to every device.

questions.q: What device connects two different local area networks (LANs) and directs data packets using IP addresses?
questions.why: Routers operate at Network Layer 3, inspecting packet destination IP addresses to route data between distinct networks.

questions.q: What is the difference between an intranet and an extranet?
o: An extranet is another name for the public internet
An intranet can be accessed by anyone on the internet
An extranet lets authorised outside users, such as suppliers, access part of an organisation's private network
There is no difference: they are the same thing
questions.why: An intranet is private to an organisation's own staff; an extranet extends controlled access to selected outside users such as suppliers or customers.

long.q: A small business wants staff working from home to use the office network securely. Explain how a VPN would help.
scheme: B1: it creates an encrypted tunnel across the internet
B1: so data that is intercepted can't be read
B1: staff appear to be on the office network, so they can use shared files and services

long.q: Compare packet switching and circuit switching for transmitting data across a wide area network (WAN).
scheme: B1: circuit switching reserves a dedicated physical communication path between sender and receiver for the entire session duration
B1: packet switching breaks data into packets, each routed independently along the best available path according to network traffic
B1: packet switching optimises bandwidth efficiency because transmission lines are shared among multiple users
B1: circuit switching guarantees constant bandwidth and zero jitter, but wastes capacity when no data is being sent

long.q: Compare a hub and a switch in a local area network.
scheme: B1: both connect several devices together in a LAN
B1: a hub sends every data packet it receives to all the connected devices
B1: a switch reads the destination (MAC) address and sends the packet only to the intended device, so there is less traffic and better security

long.q: Explain the difference between an intranet and an extranet, giving a use of each for a manufacturing company.
scheme: B1: an intranet is a private network that only the company's own employees can access
B1: use, e.g. staff handbook, internal news, timesheets, shared documents
B1: an extranet extends part of the intranet to authorised outside users such as suppliers or customers, who log in
B1: use, e.g. suppliers check stock levels and receive orders; customers track their orders

long.q: An office is choosing between wired (Ethernet) and wireless (Wi-Fi) connections for its computers. Compare the two.
scheme: B1: wired connections are usually faster and more reliable, with less interference
B1: wired connections are more secure, as a device must be physically plugged in
B1: Wi-Fi lets users move around with laptops and phones, and no cables need to be laid
B1: Wi-Fi is easier and cheaper to expand, but signals weaken through walls and with distance, and must be encrypted

questions.q: The inference engine of an expert system
o: applies rules to the knowledge base to reach conclusions
questions.why: The reasoning part.

questions.q: Which part of an expert system applies rules to the facts to reach a conclusion?
questions.why: The knowledge base holds the facts and the rule base the IF…THEN rules.

questions.q: Which is a use of an expert system?
questions.why: Others: mineral prospecting, car fault diagnosis, financial planning.

questions.q: Which component of an expert system applies logical rules to facts to deduce new conclusions?
questions.why: The inference engine is the processing mechanism that executes forward or backward chaining through the rules stored in the knowledge base.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of an expert system used for medical diagnosis?
o: It gives consistent answers every time
It can be used at any time of day
It can explain how it reached its conclusion
It cannot use common sense or deal with cases not covered by its rules
questions.why: An expert system can only apply the rules in its knowledge base, so unusual cases and human judgement are beyond it; the other options are advantages.

long.q: Describe the components of an expert system used for medical diagnosis and how it reaches a conclusion.
scheme: B1: knowledge base: facts about illnesses and symptoms
B1: rules base: IF–THEN rules
B1: inference engine applies the rules to the facts and the user's answers
B1: user interface asks questions (e.g. symptoms) and shows the diagnosis
B1: explanation system shows how the conclusion was reached, often with a probability

long.q: Describe how an expert system for identifying plant diseases would be created.
scheme: B1: the knowledge engineer gathers knowledge from experts, e.g. by interviews, and from books and research
B1: the facts are entered into the knowledge base
B1: IF–THEN rules are written into the rules base
B1: the inference engine is set up, and the user interface designed to ask questions and display results
B1: the system is tested with cases whose answers are known, and the results checked by the experts

long.q: A car garage is considering an expert system to help mechanics diagnose engine faults. Evaluate the use of the expert system.
scheme: B1: advantage: it holds the knowledge of many experts, so less experienced mechanics can diagnose faults
B1: advantage: consistent answers, faster diagnosis, and it can explain its reasoning
B1: disadvantage: expensive to set up and keep up to date with new car models
B1: disadvantage: it lacks common sense and can't handle faults outside its rules, so mechanics may rely on it too much

long.q: Explain the difference between forward chaining and backward chaining in an expert system's inference engine.
scheme: B1: forward chaining starts with the known facts (data), e.g. the symptoms
B1: it applies the rules to work forward until a conclusion is reached
B1: backward chaining starts with a possible conclusion (goal), e.g. a suspected illness
B1: it works backwards through the rules to find whether the facts support it, asking questions as needed

long.q: Give three uses of expert systems other than medical diagnosis, and for one of them describe what its knowledge base would contain.
scheme: B1: a use, e.g. mineral prospecting
B1: a second use, e.g. financial planning or investment advice
B1: a third use, e.g. car fault diagnosis, plant or animal identification, chess, insurance risk
B1: suitable knowledge base contents, e.g. for mineral prospecting: rock types and geological features linked to where minerals are found

questions.q: VLOOKUP searches
o: the first column of a table for a value and returns one from another column
questions.why: Vertical lookup.

questions.q: A spreadsheet formula should refer to:
o: A cell reference holding the value
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the formula had to reference a cell rather than a value.

questions.q: A formula is copied down a column but must keep using cell B1. Which reference is used?
questions.why: Absolute references don't change when copied.

questions.q: In a spreadsheet formula, why is $C$5 used instead of C5 when copying the formula down a column?
o: To convert the cell value into currency
To lock the reference as an absolute cell reference so it does not change
To sum all cells between C and 5
questions.why: Dollar signs create absolute references; copying a formula with $C$5 keeps the target fixed on column C and row 5.

questions.q: Cell B2 contains 50. What does =IF(B2>=70,"A",IF(B2>=50,"B","C")) return?
questions.why: 50 is not 70 or more, so the second IF is checked; 50 >= 50 is true, so it returns B.

long.q: A sheet named Prices holds product codes in A2:A50 and prices in C2:C50. On another sheet, B2 holds a product code. Write a formula for C2 that returns the matching price and can be copied down, and explain each part.
scheme: B1: =VLOOKUP(B2,Prices!$A$2:$C$50,3,FALSE)
B1: B2 is the value looked up (the product code)
B1: the absolute range stays fixed when copied; column 3 returns the price
B1: FALSE returns an exact match only

long.q: Column B (B2:B200) holds each order's region and column C (C2:C200) its value. Write a formula to calculate the total value of orders from the region North, and another to count the North orders worth more than 1000.
scheme: B1: =SUMIF(B2:B200,"North",C2:C200)
B1: =COUNTIFS(B2:B200,"North",C2:C200,">1000")
B1: both formulas use the correct ranges and criteria in quotes (the text criterion may instead refer to a cell holding North)

long.q: Explain what a named range is, describe how to create one, and give two benefits of using named ranges in formulas.
scheme: B1: a named range is a meaningful name given to a cell or group of cells, e.g. VATRate for B1
B1: select the cells and type the name in the name box, or use Define Name
B1: benefit: formulas are easier to read and understand, e.g. =A2*VATRate
B1: benefit: a name works as an absolute reference, so it stays correct when the formula is copied

long.q: Cells D2:D50 hold monthly profit, and F1 holds a target. Describe how to use conditional formatting so that losses show in red and profits at or above the target show in green.
scheme: B1: select D2:D50 and add a conditional formatting rule
B1: rule: cell value less than 0 → red text or fill
B1: second rule: cell value greater than or equal to =$F$1 → green, referring to the target cell absolutely

long.q: A spreadsheet model calculates profit in B10 from a selling price in B2. Describe how to use Goal Seek to find the selling price needed to make a profit of 5000, and explain what Goal Seek does.
scheme: B1: open Goal Seek (a what-if analysis tool)
B1: set cell: B10, to value: 5000
B1: by changing cell: B2
B1: Goal Seek repeatedly tries values of the input cell until the formula cell reaches the target value, then shows that input value

questions.q: A foreign key
o: links a record to the primary key of another table
is unique in its own table
questions.why: Used to create relationships.

questions.q: Normalisation aims to
questions.why: Removes repeated data and anomalies.

questions.q: In normalisation to third normal form, a table must have:
o: No non-key field that depends on another non-key field
questions.why: Examiners (2023): descriptions of normalisation often lacked detail.

questions.q: What is the purpose of third normal form (3NF) in relational database design?
o: To allow duplicate records across tables
To remove all primary keys from tables
To eliminate transitive functional dependencies between non-key attributes
To merge all database tables into a single sheet
questions.why: 3NF requires a relation to be in 2NF and have every non-key attribute depend solely on the primary key, removing transitive dependencies.

questions.q: In a school database, each class is taught by one teacher and each teacher teaches many classes. What is the relationship between TEACHER and CLASS?
questions.why: One teacher is linked to many classes but each class to only one teacher, so it is one-to-many; TeacherID would be a foreign key in CLASS.

long.q: The table Bookings(BookingID, CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerPhone, RoomNo, BookingDate) is not in third normal form. Explain why, and normalise it.
scheme: B1: CustomerName and CustomerPhone depend on CustomerID, not on the key BookingID (a non-key dependency)
B1: Customers(CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerPhone) with CustomerID as primary key
B1: Bookings(BookingID, CustomerID, RoomNo, BookingDate) with BookingID as primary key
B1: CustomerID in Bookings is a foreign key linking to Customers

long.q: Explain the concept of referential integrity in a relational database and how foreign keys enforce it.
scheme: B1: referential integrity ensures relationships between database tables remain valid and consistent
B1: a foreign key in a child table must match an existing primary key value in the referenced parent table or be null
B1: the database prevents deleting a record in the parent table if related dependent records exist in the child table
B1: preventing orphan records and ensuring data consistency across tables

long.q: Explain the three types of relationship between tables in a relational database, and how a many-to-many relationship is put into practice.
scheme: B1: one-to-one: each record in one table links to only one record in the other, e.g. a student and their locker
B1: one-to-many: one record links to many records in another table, e.g. one customer has many orders
B1: many-to-many: many records in each table link to many in the other, e.g. students and courses
B1: a link (junction) table is created holding the primary keys of both tables as foreign keys, giving two one-to-many relationships

long.q: Describe serial, sequential and direct (random) file organisation, and give a suitable use for direct access.
scheme: B1: serial: records stored one after another in the order they arrive, not sorted
B1: sequential: records stored one after another in order of a key field
B1: direct (random): the position of each record is calculated from its key (e.g. by hashing), so it can be reached without reading others
B1: a use, e.g. a booking system or stock enquiry where single records must be found instantly

long.q: Describe how to create a parameter query that asks the user for a surname and lists the matching customers, and give an advantage of a parameter query.
scheme: B1: create a query on the Customers table and add the fields needed
B1: in the criteria for Surname enter a prompt in square brackets, e.g. [Enter surname], so a box appears asking for the value when the query runs
B1: advantage: one query can be reused for any surname without being edited

questions.q: Lossy compression
o: permanently removes some data to reduce file size
questions.why: e.g. MP3, MP4.

questions.q: Why is a sound file normalised (amplified to just below the maximum)?
o: To make it as loud as possible without clipping
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many amplified past the maximum, clipping the waveform.

questions.q: What is a transition in video editing?
o: An effect used to move from one clip to the next
questions.why: Examples: fade, wipe, dissolve.

questions.q: A sound is recorded at 44 100 samples per second with a 16-bit sample resolution, in mono, for 10 seconds. What is the uncompressed file size?
questions.why: 44 100 × 16 × 10 = 7 056 000 bits, and dividing by 8 gives 882 000 bytes; a stereo recording would be twice this.

questions.q: Which video edit removes unwanted footage from the start and end of a clip?
questions.why: Trimming shortens a clip by cutting time from its start or end; cropping removes the edges of the picture instead.

long.q: Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression of an audio file, and say which you would use for a podcast streamed to mobile phones, with a reason.
scheme: B1: lossy permanently removes data (sounds people hear least), e.g. MP3
B1: lossless shrinks the file without losing data, so the original can be rebuilt exactly, e.g. FLAC
B1: lossy for the podcast
B1: smaller files stream faster and use less mobile data; for speech the loss is barely noticeable

long.q: A 3-minute stereo recording is sampled at 44.1 kHz with a sample resolution (bit depth) of 16 bits. Calculate the uncompressed file size in megabytes (1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes).
scheme: M1: bits per second = 44 100 × 16 × 2 (channels) = 1 411 200
M1: multiplies by the time in seconds: × 180

long.q: Explain the effect on an audio file of increasing (a) the sampling rate and (b) the sample resolution (bit depth).
scheme: B1: (a) more samples are taken each second, so the recording is closer to the original sound wave, especially at high frequencies
B1: (a) the file size increases in proportion to the sampling rate
B1: (b) more bits per sample means more possible amplitude levels, so each sample is more accurate with a greater dynamic range and less noise
B1: (b) the file size also increases

long.q: You have 20 minutes of raw video footage and must produce a 30-second advert. Describe the editing steps you would carry out.
scheme: B1: import the clips into the video-editing software and place them on the timeline
B1: trim/cut each clip to keep only the best parts so the total is 30 seconds
B1: add transitions between clips, e.g. a fade or dissolve
B1: add a soundtrack or voice-over, with the music fading in and out, and adjust volume levels
B1: add titles or captions, e.g. the company name, then export (render) in a suitable format and resolution

long.q: Explain what is meant by the frame rate and the resolution of a video, and the effect on the file size of increasing each.
scheme: B1: frame rate is the number of still images (frames) shown per second, e.g. 30 fps
B1: a higher frame rate gives smoother motion but more frames to store, so a larger file
B1: resolution is the number of pixels in each frame, e.g. 1920 × 1080
B1: a higher resolution gives a sharper picture but more data per frame, so a larger file

questions.q: Augmented reality
o: overlays digital content on the real world
questions.why: VR replaces; AR overlays.

questions.q: Which is an emerging technology?
questions.why: Others include 3D printing, virtual reality and AI.

questions.q: What is augmented reality?
o: Computer images laid over a live view of the real world
questions.why: Virtual reality replaces the real view completely.

questions.q: A hospital wants to make a prosthetic hand that exactly fits one patient, using a 3D scan of the patient's arm. Which technology is most suitable?
questions.why: 3D printing builds an object layer by layer from a digital model, so a part can be customised cheaply for a single patient.

questions.q: Trainee pilots wear headsets showing a fully computer-generated cockpit that blocks out the real room. Which technology is this?
questions.why: Virtual reality immerses the user in a completely simulated environment; augmented reality would add images on top of the real surroundings.

long.q: Discuss the use of augmented reality (AR) in education.
scheme: B1: AR overlays computer-generated images on the real world, seen through a phone, tablet or headset
B1: benefit: makes abstract ideas visible, e.g. 3D models of organs or molecules
B1: benefit: interactive and engaging; safe practice of tasks
B1: drawback: cost of devices and content; not every student has a suitable device
B1: drawback: can distract; eye strain or motion sickness
B1: a reasoned conclusion

long.q: Discuss the impact of 3D printing on manufacturing and medicine.
scheme: B1: 3D printing builds objects layer by layer from a digital (CAD) model
B1: manufacturing: prototypes can be made quickly and cheaply, speeding up product development
B1: manufacturing: customised or spare parts made on demand, reducing stock and transport
B1: medicine: custom prosthetics, implants and dental crowns made to fit the individual patient
B1: drawbacks: slow for mass production; materials can be expensive; risk of copying designs or printing weapons
B1: a reasoned conclusion

long.q: Explain how quantum cryptography makes the exchange of an encryption key more secure.
scheme: B1: the key is sent as a stream of photons, each with a polarisation representing a bit (quantum key distribution)
B1: measuring a photon changes its state, so it cannot be read without being disturbed
B1: an eavesdropper therefore introduces errors that the sender and receiver can detect by comparing part of the key
B1: if errors are found, the key is discarded and a new one sent, so a key in use has not been intercepted

long.q: Discuss the use of wearable computing devices, such as smartwatches and fitness trackers, in health care.
scheme: B1: sensors monitor heart rate, activity, sleep or blood oxygen continuously
B1: data can be sent to doctors, allowing remote monitoring of patients with long-term conditions
B1: they can alert the wearer or emergency services, e.g. irregular heartbeat or a fall
B1: drawbacks: readings may be inaccurate; privacy and security of health data; cost; people may rely on them instead of seeing a doctor
B1: a reasoned conclusion

long.q: Evaluate the use of computer-assisted translation (CAT) software by professional translators.
scheme: B1: CAT tools store previously translated sentences in a translation memory and suggest them when similar text appears
B1: a terminology database keeps technical terms consistent across documents
B1: the translator works faster, and large documents are translated more cheaply and consistently
B1: drawbacks: suggestions may not fit the context, idioms or tone, so a human translator must still check and edit; software and memory cost
B1: a reasoned conclusion

topics.name: Role and impact of IT in society

questions.q: Which is an impact of online banking on society?
o: fewer bank branches and less face-to-face service
questions.why: Convenience with social costs.

questions.q: Which is a negative impact of IT on employment?
o: Some jobs are replaced by automation
questions.why: Discuss both sides when asked about impact.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of online banking for customers?
o: Banking at any time without travelling
questions.why: Answer from the viewpoint the question asks for.

questions.q: Which is a likely effect of using robots on a car production line?
o: More workers are needed to paint cars by hand
Consistent quality and continuous production, but fewer manual jobs
Each car is built to a slightly different standard
questions.why: Robots work non-stop to the same precision, which raises output and quality, but they replace many manual workers.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of online learning for students?
o: It depends on having a reliable internet connection
There is less face-to-face contact with teachers
It can be harder to stay motivated
Students can study at their own pace and at any time
questions.why: Online materials are available whenever and wherever the student chooses; the other options are disadvantages.

long.q: Evaluate the impact of online shopping on customers and on high-street shops.
scheme: B1: customers: wider choice and easy price comparison
B1: customers: shop at any time with home delivery, helpful for people with limited mobility
B1: customers: risk of fraud, can't inspect goods, returns are less convenient
B1: shops: fewer visitors, leading to closures and job losses
B1: shops that adapt, e.g. click-and-collect or their own websites
B1: a reasoned judgement

long.q: Evaluate the impact of online banking on customers and on banks.
scheme: B1: customers: can bank at any time and from anywhere, without travelling or queueing
B1: customers: easy to check balances, transfer money and pay bills, helping them manage money
B1: customers: risk of fraud such as phishing; people without internet access or skills are excluded; less personal contact
B1: banks: fewer branches and staff needed, reducing costs
B1: banks: must invest in security systems and deal with fraud; branch staff lose jobs
B1: a reasoned judgement

long.q: Discuss the impact of social networking on the way businesses market their products.
scheme: B1: businesses can reach very large audiences cheaply, with posts shared by users
B1: adverts can be targeted at people by age, location or interests, using their data
B1: businesses can talk directly with customers and get instant feedback
B1: negative reviews and complaints can spread quickly and harm the brand; content must be managed constantly
B1: a reasoned conclusion

long.q: Evaluate the impact of online learning (e-learning) on students.
scheme: B1: students can learn at their own pace, at any time and in any place
B1: access to a wide range of courses and resources, e.g. videos and interactive quizzes, often cheaply
B1: suits people who cannot attend in person, e.g. through work, illness or distance
B1: drawbacks: less face-to-face contact and support from teachers and classmates
B1: drawbacks: needs self-discipline, a device and a reliable internet connection
B1: a reasoned judgement

long.q: Evaluate the impact of computer-controlled robots on manufacturing workers and companies.
scheme: B1: companies: robots work 24 hours a day without breaks, increasing output
B1: companies: consistent quality and fewer errors; lower long-term labour costs
B1: companies: high initial cost of robots, programming and maintenance
B1: workers: many unskilled jobs are lost
B1: workers: new skilled jobs in programming and maintaining robots; dangerous, repetitive tasks are removed
B1: a reasoned judgement

questions.q: TCP/IP is
o: the set of protocols the internet uses
questions.why: Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol.

questions.q: What is a WAN?
o: A network covering a large geographical area
questions.why: The internet is the largest WAN.

questions.q: Which transmission medium is least affected by electrical interference?
questions.why: It carries light rather than electrical signals.

questions.q: What topology connects all network nodes to a central switch or hub?
questions.why: In a star network, each device has its own point-to-point cable to a central switch, preventing single-cable failure from bringing down the network.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a mesh topology?
o: If one link fails, data can be sent by another route
It is the cheapest topology to install
It needs no network interface cards
questions.why: Each node has several connections, so data can be re-routed around a broken link; the extra cabling makes it expensive.

long.q: Two office buildings 2 km apart are to be connected. Compare fibre-optic cable with copper cable for this link.
scheme: B1: fibre has much higher bandwidth
B1: fibre carries signals much further with less attenuation, so fewer repeaters
B1: fibre is unaffected by electromagnetic interference and is harder to tap
B1: copper is cheaper and easier to install but suits shorter runs, so fibre suits 2 km

long.q: Describe the roles of TCP and IP when a file is sent across the internet.
scheme: B1: TCP breaks the file into packets, numbering each one
B1: IP adds the source and destination IP addresses and routes each packet across the networks
B1: packets may travel by different routes and arrive out of order
B1: TCP at the receiver reassembles the packets in order, checks for errors and requests any missing packets

long.q: Compare the POP3 and IMAP protocols for receiving email.
scheme: B1: both are protocols used to retrieve email from a mail server
B1: POP3 downloads messages to one device and usually deletes them from the server
B1: IMAP keeps messages on the server and synchronises them, so they can be read on several devices
B1: POP3 lets mail be read offline and uses little server storage; IMAP needs a connection and more server space

long.q: Explain how a peer-to-peer protocol such as BitTorrent distributes a large file to many users.
scheme: B1: the file is split into many small pieces
B1: a user's client gets a list of peers holding the file from a tracker (or torrent file)
B1: it downloads different pieces from many peers at the same time
B1: as soon as it has pieces it uploads them to other peers, so no single server carries all the load

long.q: Explain how a firewall protects a company's network.
scheme: B1: a firewall sits between the company network and the internet and examines all incoming and outgoing traffic
B1: it compares each packet with a set of rules, e.g. allowed IP addresses, ports or protocols
B1: packets that do not meet the rules are blocked
B1: e.g. it can block access to certain websites, log traffic and warn of attempted intrusions

questions.q: A Gantt chart shows
questions.why: Used to schedule and track a project.

questions.q: The critical path is
o: the longest sequence of dependent tasks
questions.why: It sets the shortest possible project duration.

questions.q: In project management, a deliverable is:
o: A resource delivered for a task
A measurable output produced at the end of a stage
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many described deliverables as resources that had to be delivered.

questions.q: In project management, what is defined by the critical path in a PERT or CPM chart?
o: The list of non-essential project tasks
The sequence of dependent tasks that determines the shortest possible project completion time
The longest break period between milestones
questions.why: Any delay to an activity on the critical path directly delays the completion date of the entire project.

questions.q: A project has tasks A (3 days); B (4 days, after A); C (2 days, after A); D (5 days, after both B and C). What is the shortest time to complete the project?
questions.why: The critical path is A, B, D: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 days. C runs alongside B, so the total is not the sum of all the tasks (14).

long.q: Explain how a Gantt chart helps a project manager.
scheme: B1: shows each task against a timeline
B1: shows dependencies and the critical path
B1: helps allocate resources and spot clashes
B1: progress can be tracked against the plan

long.q: Describe the five stages of project management.
scheme: B1: initiation: the aims, scope and feasibility of the project are agreed
B1: planning: tasks, timescales, resources and budget are planned, e.g. with Gantt or PERT charts
B1: execution: the team carries out the tasks in the plan
B1: monitoring and control: progress is checked against the plan and changes made to keep to time and budget
B1: close: the project is handed over, reviewed and evaluated

long.q: A project has five tasks. A takes 3 days and has no predecessor. B takes 5 days and C takes 2 days; both follow A. D takes 4 days and follows C. E takes 2 days and follows both B and D. Find the critical path, the minimum duration of the project and the float of task B.
scheme: M1: finds the lengths of both paths: A–B–E = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 days; A–C–D–E = 3 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 11 days
A1: critical path A–C–D–E
A1: minimum duration 11 days
B1: float of B = 11 − 10 = 1 day
long.ans: critical path A–C–D–E; 11 days; float of B = 1 day

long.q: Describe four features of project management software that help a project manager.
scheme: B1: scheduling: produces Gantt charts and critical paths automatically
B1: resource allocation: assigns staff and equipment to tasks and flags clashes
B1: budgeting: tracks costs against the budget
B1: e.g. collaboration and communication tools; progress tracking with alerts for missed deadlines; reports for stakeholders

long.q: Explain what is meant by scope creep and describe two ways a project manager can control it.
scheme: B1: scope creep is when extra features or requirements are added during a project without proper planning, causing delays and overspending
B1: a way, e.g. agree a clear, signed-off scope document at the start
B1: a second way, e.g. a formal change-control process in which every change is assessed for cost and time before it is approved

questions.q: Black-box testing checks
o: inputs and outputs without looking at the code
questions.why: White-box testing looks at internal logic.

questions.q: In the system life cycle, what happens during analysis?
o: The current system is studied and requirements are identified
questions.why: Methods include interviews, questionnaires and observation.

questions.q: Which changeover method runs the old and new systems together?
questions.why: It is safe but costly in time and staff.

questions.q: A supermarket chain introduces a new system in one branch first, and in the other branches only once it is working well. Which implementation method is this?
questions.why: Pilot running tries the whole system in one location first; phased implementation brings in one part of the system at a time across the organisation.

questions.q: Which item is found in technical documentation but not usually in user documentation?
o: What to do if an error message appears
questions.why: Technical documentation is for the people who maintain the system, so it includes code, file structures and data dictionaries; user documentation explains how to use it.

long.q: Describe three methods of investigating the current system during analysis, giving an advantage of each.
scheme: B1: questionnaires
B1: reach many users quickly; anonymous answers may be more honest
B1: interviews
B1: follow-up questions give detailed answers
B1: observation (or examining documents)
B1: shows what really happens rather than what people say happens

long.q: Compare the waterfall and agile approaches to developing a new system.
scheme: B1: waterfall: each stage of the life cycle is completed before the next begins, in a fixed order
B1: waterfall: the requirements are fixed at the start, with clear documentation and easy-to-measure progress
B1: waterfall: changes are hard and costly late on, and the user sees the system only near the end
B1: agile: the system is built in short iterations (sprints), each delivering working parts
B1: agile: users are involved throughout and changes in requirements are welcomed
B1: agile: less documentation and harder to predict final cost and time; suits projects with changing requirements

long.q: Describe corrective, adaptive and perfective maintenance, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: corrective maintenance fixes errors (bugs) found after the system is in use
B1: example, e.g. correcting a calculation that gives the wrong total
B1: adaptive maintenance changes the system to suit new circumstances
B1: example, e.g. a new tax law, a new operating system or new hardware
B1: perfective maintenance improves the performance or features of a working system
B1: example, e.g. making searches faster or adding a feature users request

long.q: Explain the difference between alpha testing and beta testing.
scheme: B1: alpha testing is carried out by the developers (or in-house testers) at the developer's site
B1: it takes place before the system is released, to find and fix as many errors as possible
B1: beta testing is carried out by a selected group of real users in their own environment
B1: it finds problems missed in alpha testing, and the users' feedback is used to improve the final version

long.q: Describe pilot implementation and phased implementation of a new system, and give a situation where each is suitable.
scheme: B1: pilot: the new system is introduced fully in one branch or department first, and then everywhere once it works
B1: suitable for, e.g. a supermarket chain with many similar branches
B1: phased: the new system is introduced one part (module) at a time, replacing the old one gradually
B1: suitable for, e.g. a system made of separate modules such as payroll then stock control

questions.q: Vector graphics
questions.why: Stored as shapes and paths.

questions.q: Why are vector graphics better than bitmaps for a logo?
o: They can be resized without losing quality
questions.why: Vectors are stored as shapes and coordinates.

questions.q: What does increasing an image's resolution do?
o: Increases the number of pixels and the file size
questions.why: Higher resolution means more detail.

questions.q: An uncompressed bitmap is 1000 × 800 pixels with a 24-bit colour depth. What is its file size? (1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes)
questions.why: 1000 × 800 × 24 = 19 200 000 bits; dividing by 8 gives 2 400 000 bytes, which is 2.4 MB.

questions.q: Why are layers used in graphics editing software?
o: To edit or move parts of an image independently of the others
To convert a bitmap into a vector graphic
questions.why: Elements on separate layers can be changed, hidden or moved without affecting the rest of the image; keeping layers usually makes the file bigger, not smaller.

long.q: Explain why a company logo should be created as a vector graphic rather than a bitmap.
scheme: B1: a vector stores shapes as mathematical objects (lines, curves, fills), not pixels
B1: it scales to any size without pixelation, from business card to billboard
B1: the file is usually smaller, and each shape is easy to edit

long.q: Explain what layers are in graphics-editing software and give two benefits of using them.
scheme: B1: layers are separate, transparent sheets stacked on top of each other, each holding part of the image
B1: benefit: each element can be edited, moved or hidden without affecting the rest
B1: benefit: e.g. order of objects easily changed; effects such as opacity applied to one layer; easier to undo mistakes

long.q: Describe how to remove the background from a photograph of a product and place the product on a plain coloured background.
scheme: B1: use a selection tool, e.g. magic wand, lasso or quick-selection, to select the product (or the background)
B1: refine the selection edges, then delete the background or apply a layer mask
B1: add a new layer below the product and fill it with the chosen colour
B1: save in the software's own format with layers, and export, e.g. as .png or .jpg

long.q: A photograph is to be printed at 6 inches by 4 inches at 300 pixels per inch. Calculate the number of pixels needed, and the uncompressed file size in megabytes with 24-bit colour (1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes).
scheme: M1: multiplies each dimension by 300: 6 × 300 = 1800 and 4 × 300 = 1200
M1: 24 bits = 3 bytes per pixel: 2 160 000 × 3

long.q: Describe how a shape in a vector graphic is edited using nodes and paths, and how grouping objects helps when creating a logo.
scheme: B1: a vector shape is made of paths that join points called nodes (anchor points)
B1: dragging a node moves that point and changes the shape
B1: the handles on a node change the curve of the path (Bézier curves); nodes can be added or deleted
B1: grouping joins several objects so they move, resize and scale together as one, keeping the logo's proportions

questions.q: In animation, tweening
questions.why: In-betweening.

questions.q: What is tweening in animation?
o: Generating the frames between two key frames
questions.why: It saves time and makes motion smooth.

questions.q: Frame rate is measured in:
questions.why: A higher frame rate gives smoother motion.

questions.q: An animation runs at 12 frames per second for 5 seconds. Frames 1 and 60 are key frames and tweening creates the rest. How many frames does the software generate?
questions.why: 12 × 5 = 60 frames in total; two of them are the key frames drawn by the animator, so 58 are generated.

questions.q: A circle gradually changes into a square over 30 frames. Which technique produces this?
o: Frame-by-frame animation with no key frames
questions.why: Shape tweening generates the in-between frames that change one shape into another; motion tweening changes position, size or rotation but keeps the shape.

long.q: Explain what tweening is and how it saves time compared with frame-by-frame animation. An animation lasts 4 seconds at 24 frames per second: how many frames does it have?
scheme: B1: the animator sets key frames (e.g. start and end positions)
B1: the software generates the in-between frames
B1: so far fewer frames are drawn by hand, and motion is smooth
B1: 4 × 24 = 96 frames

long.q: Explain what morphing is in animation and how it differs from a motion tween.
scheme: B1: morphing (a shape tween) gradually changes one shape into a different shape over a series of frames
B1: the software generates the in-between shapes from the start and end key frames
B1: a motion tween changes an object's position, size, rotation or colour but keeps the same shape

long.q: Explain what onion skinning is and why it is useful when creating frame-by-frame animation.
scheme: B1: onion skinning shows faint (semi-transparent) images of the previous and/or next frames behind the current frame
B1: the animator can see where the object was, so the next drawing is placed in the right position
B1: so the movement is smooth and consistent, without jumps

long.q: Explain the purpose of the timeline and of layers in animation software.
scheme: B1: the timeline shows the frames in order, with time running from left to right
B1: key frames and tweens are set on the timeline, which controls when each change happens and for how long
B1: layers hold different objects, e.g. the background on one layer and a character on another
B1: so each object can be animated independently, and the stacking order decides which appears in front

long.q: Describe how to animate a ball so it follows a curved path and slows down as it reaches the end.
scheme: B1: draw the ball and convert it into a symbol (object) on its own layer
B1: draw a curved motion path (guide) on a guide layer
B1: set key frames at the start and end with the ball snapped to each end of the path, and apply a motion tween
B1: apply easing out (ease-out) so the ball decelerates towards the end

questions.q: JavaScript in a web page is mainly used to
questions.why: HTML structure, CSS style, JavaScript behaviour.

questions.q: Which language adds interactivity to a web page in the browser?
questions.why: HTML is structure; CSS is presentation.

questions.q: In JavaScript, setInterval(f, 1000) runs f:
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates left a timer at the default 1000 ms instead of the value required.

questions.q: What value is shown? var t = 0; for (var i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { t = t + i; } alert(t);
questions.why: i takes the values 1, 2, 3 and 4 (the loop runs while i <= 4), so t = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

questions.q: In JavaScript, what is the result of "5" + 3?
questions.why: When + has a string operand, JavaScript turns the number into a string and joins them, giving "53"; Number("5") + 3 would give 8.

long.q: Write JavaScript so that clicking the button with id 'go' changes the text of the paragraph with id 'msg' to 'Hello'.
scheme: B1: select the button: document.getElementById("go")
B1: attach a click handler: addEventListener("click", …) or onclick
B1: select the paragraph: document.getElementById("msg")
B1: set its innerHTML (or textContent) to "Hello"

long.q: Write a JavaScript function called area that takes a width and a height and returns their product, and code that shows the result of area(4, 5) in the element with id 'out'.
scheme: B1: function area(w, h) { … } with two parameters
B1: return w * h;

questions.q: A mail merge field
o: is replaced with data from the source for each record
is a fixed piece of text
questions.why: e.g. «FirstName».

questions.q: What is a mail merge?
o: Combining a standard document with a data source to make personalised copies
Sending one email to one person
questions.why: Merge fields are replaced by data from each record.

questions.q: How can a mail merge send letters only to customers in one city?
o: Filter the data source on the City field
questions.why: Filters select records without changing the data.

questions.q: Letters should begin 'Dear Sir' or 'Dear Madam' depending on the Title field in the data source. Which mail merge feature does this?
o: A filter on the data source
Sorting the data source by Title
A fill-in field typed in at each merge
questions.why: An IF…THEN…ELSE rule checks a field's value for each record and inserts the matching text; a filter only chooses which records are merged.

questions.q: Why should the merged letters be previewed before printing 500 of them?
o: To check that the merge fields are placed correctly and the data appears as expected
To remove duplicate records from the data source
To send the letters automatically by email
To sort the data source into order
questions.why: Previewing shows real data in the letters, so problems such as missing spaces, wrong fields or badly formatted dates can be fixed before paper is wasted.

B1: preview to check, then merge only the selected records to print or email

long.q: Explain the purpose of a Skip Record If rule and of a Fill-in (Ask) field in a mail merge, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: Skip Record If leaves out any record that meets a stated condition when merging
B1: example, e.g. skip the record if Balance equals 0, so only customers who owe money get the letter
B1: a Fill-in field asks the user to type a value when the merge runs, which is inserted into the document
B1: example, e.g. typing the date of an event or a personal comment for each letter or for all letters
